title: Confirmation
hook: many Reform communities hold confirmation at Shavuot

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was never too late: the grown-up standing at the Torah long after thirteen. What did you start late, or want to? Today, a ceremony for teenagers who have already had theirs. Day one thousand three hundred two.

A row of teenagers stands in front of the ark, a little dressed up, a little nervous. Their bar and bat mitzvahs are behind them. Since then they kept coming to a class, arguing about God, justice, and what they actually think. Now, on the holiday of Shavuot, each one stands up and says something in front of their families and the whole congregation. In many Reform communities this is called confirmation. Two questions sit inside it. Why this holiday? And why a ceremony after the one at thirteen?
screen: `TEENAGERS IN FRONT OF THE ARK.` → `ON SHAVUOT.` → `WHY HERE, AND WHY AGAIN?`

segments.voice: Confirmation. Turn it four ways. First, the holiday. Jewish tradition links Shavuot to the giving of the Torah at Sinai. In Exodus, when Moses brings God's words down to the people, they answer together that they will do all of it. So a confirmation class is standing, in a way, where that crowd stood: as a group, saying yes. Second, the order of the words. A few chapters later the people say it again. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew, na'aseh v'nishma: we will do, and we will hear. The Talmud tells of a heavenly voice praising Israel for this, for promising the doing before the hearing. Some readers take it as a picture of how commitment grows: you start living it, and the understanding comes along the way. Third, why again. At bar or bat mitzvah, the tradition says to a young person: you are now responsible. Confirmation lets an older teenager answer back, in their own words, about what they plan to do with that. The first yes is received. The second is chosen. Fourth, the book read on Shavuot. In synagogues on this holiday, the book of Ruth is read. Ruth is not born into the people she joins. She chooses them, out loud, on a road, to her mother-in-law: "whither thou goest, I will go." On the same holiday, Sinai's yes and Ruth's yes sit side by side. Confirmed, then, is not the end of learning. It's a promise made a second time, once you know a little more of what it costs.
screen: `SHAVUOT REMEMBERS SINAI.` · `WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.` · `THE FIRST YES, THEN THE SECOND.` · `RUTH CHOOSES ON A ROAD.` · then, large: `CONFIRMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recommit to something. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you said yes to a while ago: a friendship, a practice, a job, a cause, a promise to yourself. You said yes before you knew everything it would ask. Now look at it as it is today, knowing what you know. Notice what in it is still worth choosing. If something is, say yes to it again, quietly, the way the class does on Shavuot. If you pray, you can carry the words from Sinai into the quiet: we will do, and we will hear. The bell holds the time.

Confirmation: a second yes, said at Shavuot. And a week closes: the firstborn redeemed, the first haircut, honey on the letters, coming of age, teaching at thirteen, never too late, and confirmed. Today's word.
Your line: confirmed. Today, pick one thing you already said yes to, and tell someone you're still in. Day one thousand three hundred two.

howItsDone: In many Reform congregations, teenagers who have continued studying after bar or bat mitzvah are confirmed as a class on Shavuot, the holiday that remembers the giving of the Torah, often speaking or leading parts of the service.
